explanation:
## The program

```cpp
std::string line{};
std::getline(std::cin, line);

std::string result{};
for (std::size_t i = line.size(); i > 0; --i)
{
    result += line[i - 1];
}

std::cout << result << "\n";
```

## getline against >>

```
input:  hello world

std::cin >> s                 s is "hello"
std::getline(std::cin, s)     s is "hello world"
```

`>>` treats whitespace as a separator and skips it; `getline` treats
the newline as a terminator and keeps everything before it. Mixing
the two is the classic trap: after `std::cin >> n`, the newline you
pressed is still in the buffer, so the next `getline` returns an
empty string. The usual fix is `std::cin.ignore()` before the
`getline`, and the better fix is not to mix them in one program
unless you must.

## The unsigned countdown

This is the real content of the exercise.

```cpp
for (std::size_t i = line.size() - 1; i >= 0; --i)   // broken
```

Two things are wrong with it at once. On an **empty** line,
`size()` is 0, and 0 minus 1 in an unsigned type does not go
negative — it wraps to 18,446,744,073,709,551,615. The loop then
indexes far past the end of the string.

And even on a non-empty line, `i >= 0` is **always true** for an
unsigned `i`, so after `i` reaches 0 the next `--i` wraps and the
loop keeps going. Compilers warn about that one if you ask
(`-Wtype-limits`); nothing warns about the first.

Two ways out:

```cpp
for (std::size_t i = line.size(); i > 0; --i)   result += line[i - 1];
for (int i = static_cast<int>(line.size()) - 1; i >= 0; --i) result += line[i];
```

The first keeps the unsigned type and never lets it reach the
dangerous value; the second converts to a signed type where
subtracting past zero behaves as expected. The first is preferred
because it needs no cast.

## Why unsigned at all

`size()` returns `std::size_t` because a size cannot be negative
and the type can therefore address twice as much memory. The cost
is exactly this family of bugs, and it is widely regarded as a
mistake in the standard library’s design — one it is far too late
to change. Knowing that the type is unsigned, and that unsigned
subtraction wraps rather than going negative, is the defence.

## Building rather than reversing in place

Reversing in place is possible — swap the ends and walk inwards —
and is what `std::reverse` from `<algorithm>` does. Building a
second string is easier to be sure about and costs one extra copy
of a 200-character string, which is nothing.

## What this does not check

Anything beyond ASCII. Reversing a UTF-8 string byte by byte takes
multi-byte characters apart and produces invalid text — the
characters of a string and its bytes are not the same thing, and
`std::string` indexes bytes. The constraint says printable ASCII so
the exercise can stay about loops and indices.
